Leg-pain intensity in primary-care patients with sciatica

Dataset 2: Sciatica in primary care

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

In sciatica it is leg pain, not back pain, that defines the syndrome and that patients most want relieved; leg-pain intensity is the primary outcome in most sciatica trials and one of the few things a GP can act on at the first visit. These data come from a cross-sectional diagnostic study of 395 adults presenting to Dutch general practices with a new episode of sciatica, each of whom had a standardised history, a physical examination and a lumbar MRI (Verwoerd et al.; sciatica in general practice, MRI substudy). Knowing which history items and examination findings mark out the patients in most leg pain tells us whether severity is something the consultation can identify or whether it is essentially unexplained by the routine assessment.

Aim. Among primary-care patients presenting with sciatica, we examined which of age, sex, concurrent back-pain intensity, duration of the leg-pain episode, pain radiating below the knee, leg pain being worse than back pain, a positive neural-tension test and nerve-root compression on MRI are independently associated with leg-pain intensity, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. Cross-sectional baseline data from a primary-care sciatica cohort: 395 adults consulting Dutch general practitioners with a new episode of sciatica, all assessed at a single occasion. Age ranged from 19 to 82 years.

Variables. The outcome is leg_pain_intensity, average leg-pain intensity on a 0-10 numerical rating scale, where higher means worse pain. Predictors are age_yrs (years), sex (reference: female, the larger group), back_pain_intensity (0-10 numerical rating scale), leg_pain_duration (reference: under 6 weeks, the largest group), below_knee_pain (pain extends below the knee; reference: no), leg_pain_worse (patient reports leg pain worse than back pain; reference: no), neural_tension_positive (at least one positive neural-tension test; reference: no) and mri_nerve_root_compression (nerve-root compression visible on MRI; reference: no).

Two predictor choices need justification. First, back_pain_intensity is entered even though it is a pain measure like the outcome. They are related but distinct: back pain and leg pain are separately elicited on separate scales, they correlate r = 0.62 rather than 1, and 48% of patients report more back pain than leg pain. Including it answers a sharper question – which findings mark out severe leg pain over and above a patient’s general pain level – and excluding it would leave every other coefficient confounded by overall pain reporting. Second, leg_pain_worse is a patient’s own comparison of the two sites, not an arithmetic recoding of the two scores: it agrees with the sign of leg_pain_intensity - back_pain_intensity in only 71% of patients, so it carries independent information and is not a deterministic function of the outcome.

id is a participant label and is excluded from every model. clinician_sciatica – the GP’s high-confidence diagnosis – is deliberately not used. It is a summary judgement built from the same examination findings that appear as predictors here, correlating 0.61 with neural_tension_positive and 0.54 with below_knee_pain; putting it in the same model as those signs would make their coefficients uninterpretable.

Statistical analysis. Linear regression (lm()), justified because the outcome is a numerical rating scale spread across its full 0-10 range and close to symmetric. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model() plus formal tests of heteroscedasticity, residual normality and collinearity; HC3 robust standard errors via lmtest::coeftest() with sandwich::vcovHC() are reported as a sensitivity check because the outcome is bounded. Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 376 of 395 rows were analysed (19 dropped, 4.8%). Missingness in the file is confined to leg_pain_duration (19), bmi (2), back_pain_duration (2). The outcome is complete; essentially all the loss here comes from leg_pain_duration, the single most incomplete column in the dataset. This is the largest complete-case loss of the three outcomes analysed for this dataset, and it is entirely a consequence of including that one predictor.

The analysed sample has a median leg-pain intensity of 5.3/10 with the interquartile range spanning 3.7 to 7, so leg pain is moderate to severe in most patients but far from uniformly maximal. Clinical signs are common: 71% report pain below the knee, 62% have a positive neural-tension test and 60% have nerve-root compression on MRI. Only about half say their leg pain is worse than their back pain, which is a reminder that “sciatica” in primary care is often a mixed back-and-leg presentation.

Exploratory figure

Figure 1. Leg-pain intensity against back-pain intensity, split by whether the patient reports leg pain as worse than back pain. The dashed line is equality; the solid line is a linear smooth with a 95% confidence band. Points are jittered because both scales are recorded in thirds of a point.

Leg pain and back pain rise together with a slope well below the line of equality, and the whole cloud shifts upward by roughly a point when the patient says their leg pain is the worse of the two – but the two panels overlap substantially, confirming that leg_pain_worse is a self-report rather than a recoding of which number is larger.

Back-pain intensity is by far the strongest crude predictor: each additional point of back pain is associated with a 0.69-point higher leg-pain score (95% CI 0.6 to 0.78, p < 0.001), and on its own it accounts for R² = 0.39 of the variance in leg pain. Among the clinical variables, patients who report their leg pain as worse than their back pain score 1.72 points higher (95% CI 1.27 to 2.17, p < 0.001), pain below the knee carries 1.7 points (p < 0.001), a positive neural-tension test 1.57 points (p < 0.001) and nerve-root compression on MRI 1.17 points (p < 0.001). Age, sex and leg-pain duration show no crude association: the age slope is 0.014 points per year (p = 0.116), and patients in their first six weeks report much the same leg pain as those beyond twelve.

Why adjustment is needed

The crude estimates conflate a patient’s specific sciatic pain with how much pain they report in general. back_pain_intensity is the clearest confounder of every clinical sign: patients with a positive neural-tension test have mean back pain 5.7 versus 5.2 in those without, and back pain is strongly associated with leg pain (r = 0.63), so part of the crude neural-tension association is simply that patients with more pain everywhere are more likely to flinch on examination. leg_pain_worse is a second confounder, this time of the anatomical signs: it correlates with below_knee_pain (61% of patients with below-knee pain say leg pain is worse, versus 25% of those without) and is itself strongly associated with leg-pain intensity, so the crude below-knee estimate partly reflects the patient’s own ranking of their two pains. age_yrs is a third, milder one: older patients are more likely to have nerve-root compression on MRI (r = 0.1) and report slightly more leg pain, so a little of the crude MRI association is age. Adjustment converts “patients with a positive neural-tension test have worse leg pain” into the more useful “at the same back-pain level, age and pain ranking, a positive neural-tension test still marks out worse leg pain”.

Adjusting for all eight predictors, back-pain intensity remains overwhelmingly the strongest association: conditional on everything else, each extra point of back pain is associated with a 0.68-point higher leg-pain score (95% CI 0.6 to 0.75, p < 0.001). Three clinical variables remain independently associated. Reporting leg pain as worse than back pain adds 1.24 points (95% CI 0.87 to 1.61, p < 0.001), pain below the knee adds 0.88 points (p < 0.001), and nerve-root compression on MRI adds 0.45 points (p = 0.012). The neural-tension test is now only marginally associated (0.4 points, p = 0.033). Age retains a small association (0.015 points per year, p = 0.011); sex and leg-pain duration contribute nothing.

The model explains R² = 0.593 (adjusted R² = 0.583) with 37.6 observations per estimated parameter. That R² looks impressive but is mostly borrowed: dropping back_pain_intensity alone takes it from 0.59 to 0.24, so the seven clinical and demographic predictors together explain only about 24% of the variance in leg-pain intensity. The honest reading is that the consultation explains leg-pain severity poorly unless you are allowed to ask how much back pain the patient also has.

Three estimates move substantially, all toward the null. The neural-tension test collapses from 1.57 points crude to 0.4 adjusted – a 74% attenuation – and drops from p < 0.001 to p = 0.033; its crude association was largely the general-pain confounding described above, and it is the one predictor whose significance is genuinely fragile. Pain below the knee halves from 1.7 to 0.88 points but stays firmly significant, so radiation below the knee marks out worse leg pain even at the same overall pain level and the same self-ranked pain pattern. MRI nerve-root compression attenuates from 1.17 to 0.45 points and stays just significant – notable because it means the scan adds a little information about symptom severity beyond the history, though less than a single point of pain. Leg pain worse than back pain barely moves (1.72 to 1.24) and neither does age (0.014 to 0.015), confirming that neither is standing in for the rest of the set. Back-pain intensity actually moves slightly away from the null (0.69 to 0.68): the clinical signs were suppressing it a little, because patients with strong sciatic signs report relatively more leg pain for a given amount of back pain. No predictor gains significance on adjustment; one (neural tension) nearly loses it.

Diagnostics

Linearity. The fitted-versus-residual smooth is essentially flat and the posterior-predictive check tracks the observed distribution reasonably, though simulated values spill below 0 and above 10 where the real scale cannot go. In practice 0 of the 376 fitted values fall outside the 0-10 range, so the bound is not actually being violated at observed covariate patterns; the linear model is adequate here even though it is formally defined on the wrong support.

Homoscedasticity. Constant variance is not rejected (check_heteroscedasticity() p = 0.208), so ordinary standard errors are valid and HC3 re-estimation is not required. Because the outcome is bounded and residual spread narrows near the ceiling, robust standard errors are nevertheless reported below as a sensitivity check.

Under HC3 the neural-tension coefficient moves from p = 0.033 to p = 0.035, i.e. it sits on the 0.05 boundary either way; every other conclusion is unchanged. This is the one substantive result in the model that a reader should treat as provisional.

Normality of residuals. Formally rejected (check_normality() p = 0.006). The Q-Q plot shows mild departure in the tails, driven by the coarse recording of the 0-10 scale in thirds of a point and by the 15 patients piled at the ceiling of 10. With n = 376 the central limit theorem covers the coefficient standard errors, so the practical consequence is small, but this is a genuine assumption failure and should be reported as one rather than waved away.

Influential points. check_outliers() flags 0 observation(s) at the Cook’s-distance threshold.

Collinearity. No problem: the largest variance inflation factor is leg_pain_worse at 1.37, well under 5. leg_pain_worse and below_knee_pain are correlated but not collinear (VIF 1.37 and 1.22), and back_pain_intensity has a VIF of only 1.07 despite correlating 0.6 with the outcome – a useful reminder that VIF concerns predictor-predictor, not predictor-outcome, correlation. Excluding clinician_sciatica avoided the one genuine collinearity threat in this file.

Discussion

Among primary-care patients presenting with sciatica, leg-pain intensity is predicted overwhelmingly by how much back pain the patient also reports. Beyond that, three things independently mark out worse leg pain: the patient’s own judgement that the leg is the worse of the two sites (about 1.2 points), radiation below the knee (about 0.9 points) and nerve-root compression on MRI (about 0.5 points on the 0-10 scale). A positive neural-tension test, which looks impressive crudely, is almost entirely explained away by overall pain level. Practically, the history carries more information about leg-pain severity than the examination does, and the scan adds little: the MRI coefficient is smaller than the minimal clinically important difference on a 0-10 pain scale, which is usually put at 1.5 to 2 points. Duration of the leg-pain episode is irrelevant to severity, which argues against “how long has it been going on” as a triage question for pain intensity.

Limitations. The design is cross-sectional and all variables come from the same consultation, so the back-pain-leg-pain association cannot be given a direction and is inflated by common-method bias: the same patient rated both scales minutes apart. The R² of 0.59 is therefore not a measure of clinical predictability – strip out back pain and it falls to 0.24. Residual normality is formally violated, and the outcome is bounded at 0 and 10 with 15 patients at the ceiling, so fitted values can and do stray outside the achievable range. Complete-case analysis dropped 19 patients (4.8%), almost all of them missing leg_pain_duration; if patients who could not date their episode differ systematically in pain, the estimates are mildly biased. The file has no analgesic use, no psychological measures and no work status, all of which plausibly affect reported pain, so residual confounding is likely. All estimates are associations, not causal effects.

Future work. A repeat pain rating at three months would show whether the below-knee and MRI findings predict persistence of leg pain, which is the clinically actionable question.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Workable but weaker than disability_score. The headline R² of 0.59 is dominated by one predictor; without back_pain_intensity the model explains only 0.24. Students who include back pain will report a gratifying model and learn the wrong lesson about how predictable pain is; students who exclude it get an honest but flat result. Either way the supervisor has to raise the point.
  • Complete-case N = 376 of 395 (19 dropped, 4.8%) – the largest loss of the three outcomes, and entirely attributable to leg_pain_duration (19 missing), which then turns out to be non-significant. A good live demonstration that listwise deletion charges you for predictors before you know whether they are worth it.
  • Residual normality is rejected (p = 0.006) and the outcome is bounded and discrete: values are recorded in thirds of a point, 15 patients sit at the 10 ceiling and 1 at the 0 floor, and 0 fitted values fall outside 0-10. Homoscedasticity passes (p = 0.208), so HC3 is not required; it is shown anyway and moves the neural-tension p-value across the 0.05 line, which is worth knowing before a student stakes a conclusion on it.
  • No collinearity problem: max VIF 1.37. The clinician_sciatica trap applies here exactly as elsewhere – it correlates 0.61 with neural_tension_positive and 0.54 with below_knee_pain and must stay out of any model containing those signs.
  • Watch leg_pain_worse. It looks like it might be a deterministic recoding of leg_pain_intensity > back_pain_intensity, but it agrees with that comparison in only 71% of patients, so it is legitimate. Verify this before assuming either way – a genuinely deterministic version of this variable would have made the outcome unusable.
  • Fragile result to flag: neural_tension_positive sits at p = 0.033 adjusted and crosses 0.05 under robust SEs. Do not let a student build a discussion around it.
